Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:



Well, the current wording does not even hint at any sort of "at least"
clause.

10 GET#GEHENNA
20 IF #GEHENNA=5 THEN BURN MUKHTAR BEY

...is worded, if there are five Gehenna cards in play.

20 IF #GEHENNA>=5 THEN BURN MUKHTAR BEY

...would be worded, if there are (i) five or more, or (ii) more than
four Gehenna cards in play.

Five or more seems logical, but logic has proven to be a poor interpreter
of cards and rules on many occasions. I mean, it sucks when you need to
interpret "Five" as "Five or more" in certain cases _but_ not in others...
;(

--
Bye,

Daneel

On Thu, 28 Oct 2004 13:35:30 -0400, LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

>> 10 GET#GEHENNA
>> 20 IF #GEHENNA=5 THEN BURN MUKHTAR BEY
>>
>> ...is worded, if there are five Gehenna cards in play.
>
> No. That is worded, "If the number of Gehenna cards in play is five."

Semantic pondering:

Q: Are there five Gehenna cards in play?
A: Yes, there are. There are six Gehenna cards in play.

Q: How many Gehenna cards are in play?
A: There are five Gehenna cards in play.

Q: Are there five, or six Gehenna cards in play?
A: There are five Gehenna cards in play.

> When asking if a value (e.g. capacity) "is" a certain number, equality
> is assumed, yes.
>
> Please show a case in card text where a quantity is sought but an
> excess will not do.

This is not necessarily a player-friendly logic. Sure you can explain the
difference between quantity and value, but I still find it hard to believe
that your logic is intuitive for most non-native english speaking players.
Especially since most cards use "or more" type phrases. I guess this is
quite similar to the issue I had with Telepathic Tracking.

If most of the cards have a type of text to define (or even just to
clarify) their effects, and a few cards lack that text (even though
designer intent would be that they mean the same thing), then players
might logically assume that the wording is different because there is a
difference in effect.

Take for example everyone's favourite, RttF.

Recalled to the Founder [Gehenna:R]
Cardtype: Event
Gehenna. Do not replace as long as this card is in play.
Requires at least two other Gehenna cards in play. During each
Methuselah's untap phase, if he or she controls more than two vampires of
the same clan, he or she burns one such vampire. If that vampire's
capacity is above 5, this Methuselah becomes immune to the effects of this
card for the remainder of the game.

It requires "at least" two other Gehenna cards in play. Its effect
triggers when the Methuselah controls "more than two" vampires of the same
clan. Both phrases are completely lacking in ambivalence. Given the
abundant usage of such wording, one can't help but wonder whether the lack
of the phraseology used to confirm the acceptance of quantities greater
than listed ("more than", "at least", "or more", etc.) also means the lack
of the acceptance itself.

--
Bye,

Daneel

If you must put it this way... Yes. There are unique effects that need a
more or less verbose explanation, but even those effects often use
expressions
from a terminology. Just as all Strike cards say "Strike:" instead of
"Punch:",
"Kick:", "Slash:" or "Kaboom:", using a well-defined term ("Strike"), most
cards probably should - where possible - use the same words to mean the
same
thing, be it an actual defined term, or just concerted usage. It may be
logical to assume that if two effects are the same, they are worded the
same
way, and likewise, if there is a difference in wording on some cards, those
cards may have different effects.

Quite possible. Brevity may be the father of wit, but card texts should
(IMHO) be clear above all else, and not just in themselves, but also when
compared to other, similar cards. Kind of like how Derek Ray sort of
pointed
out that very few cards use the phrase "spend", and it, in all cases, can
be basically made equivalent to "burn" - which, if that is the case, should
probably be the uniform term used for all "burn" effects, not just the vast
majority.

Question 1) How many times may I expect to be able to get one free if I
buy one?

Question 2) Why do think the little diclaimer, "Limit 3 per customer" (or
whatever) got invented?

Answer to the second question: the same reason this subject comes up over
and over. It isn't just that Jyhad players have a perverse desire to
punish deceased ponies. There really is a small ambiguity. USUALLY, in

way ("During Happy Hour, all beers cost 1$.") - but not always.

The way we talk about "proper English" sometimes, you'd think it wasn't
just a collection of mispronounced French words tied together using poorly
understood French grammar.

Except that in English, it is the correct (albeit brief) wording.

(Assume that the following Gehenna cards are in play: The Slow
Withering, Absimilard's Army, Nightmares upon Nightmares, The Unmasking,
Becoming of Ennoia, Thirst. This totals six. ...Further assume that
the players have not thrown their hands up in the air and walked away
from the completely wrecked game yet, given those particular events.)

The following statements are TRUE:

1. There are five Gehenna cards in play.
2. There are at least five Gehenna cards in play.
3. There are some Gehenna cards in play.
4. There are six Gehenna cards in play.

The following statements are FALSE:

1. There are exactly five Gehenna cards in play.
2. There are only five Gehenna cards in play.
3. Five Gehenna cards are not in play.

The clearest wording for Mukhtar would have been to use the "at least"
terminology. However, the current wording is shorter while remaining
equally accurate. When space is at a premium, sometimes niceties must
be left by the wayside -- unless you'd like to see more cards like Fata
Amria printed?

-- Derek

A set of 6, however, includes a set of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

>By saying that 6 gehenna cards does not count as 5, you are trying to get
>around the intent of the card. Its logical to assume that 5 also equals more
>than 5.

Please don't try to continue this line of argument any further; you're
distorting the issue and misleading people. There's no assumption,
there's no letter-of-intent on the card, there's simply what the card
says.

Assuming that 5 equals more than 5 is patently ridiculous.

However, assuming that because there are 5, there are NOT 6 is ALSO
patently ridiculous, and is the entire point of the argument. And it is
simple math to say that if there are 6, there are also 5 and 1.

Yes, see the other replies on this matter. You may say that you have a
firm position in assessing the meaning of this phrase, but AFAIK you're
not a linguist any more than the rest of the posters, which leaves the
common sense part - and since the phrase is, in practice, widely used for
the "time constraint only" meaning, the ambiguity is undeniable.

This is where the rulings come in. (By the way, there would not have been

>>>> Especially since most cards use "or more" type phrases. I guess this
>>>> is
>>>> quite similar to the issue I had with Telepathic Tracking.
>>>

>>> no cards -- all cards should get by with as few clarifying phrases
>>> as possible.
>>
>> If you must put it this way... Yes.
>
> You are in a severe minority, I think (and I hope).

There are two different issues here, both relevant to the case. There is
the logical issue and there is the language issue. The logical issue says
that since the prime requirement for card texts is clarity, different
texts will probably mean different things. If you strive for brevity,
then you will do so on all cards to avoid the confusion. If something
needs to be clarified, then clarify it on all cards or no card (and
supply the rulebook or rulings).

Kind of like saying "Strike: Steal 2 Blood" on one card, and saying
"Strike: Steal 2 Blood. The blood lost due to this steal blood strike
cannot be prevented." Both are correct, and both can be used separately,
but seeing the two cards together creates confusion.

The language issue kind of enhances this problem. Players in some
countries may be native english speakers, but the rest of the world
only speaks english as a secondary (tertiary, etc.) language. In fact,
a lot of players do not speak english at all (except for the RPG/CCG
jargon). So if the "minority" refers to the part of the world which
does not speak english as a primary language, then yes, I'm possibly
representing a minority here... ;)

> When text can be clarified in-line (i.e., when card space allows clearer
> verbiage), then the clearer verbiage should be used.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <fqrno0tp3ql3greak...@4ax.com>, Blackheart

<le...@leech.com> writes:
>considering the number of vamps that have been released since Jyhad
>first came out.. it's rather telling that at most, there are less than
>2 dozen that get used...

Demonstrably not true - the tournament winning deck archive, for a
start.

Certainly, there are some very popular vampires which will show up in a
lot of decks devoted to e.g. their clan (Arika, say, in a big Ventrue
deck) or that archetype (Jimmy Dunn in various forms of combat), and so
on. But there are a wide and various scattering of vampires to be found
all over the place.

Indeed, in situations where it is only 2 dozen that get used, assuming
each Methuselah on a 5 player table brings out 3, you have a *lot* of
contestation possibilities. (Birthday Paradox maths fun, if you care to
investigate the odds.) In which case, picking the less obviously
popular vampires has a less obvious benefit than the vampire would
originally show.

Also, some vampires make very good "single vampire" possibilities. The
Fatima multi-rush deck, say, or the Turbo-Arika deck. These vampires
are the ones that tend to stick in people's memories - very much
"signature" vampires.

Additionally, I don't see any reason why all vampires should be equally
played. Some very niche vampires lurk around who are incredibly useful
when you need them in a deck, though you wouldn't necessarily use them
much anywhere else. And a fair few of the Bloodlines vampires are good
for spicing up other decks.

--
